title: Reproduction in plants
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 9 Integrated Science; not yet checked by a CBC Integrated Science teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Cut real flowers open (hibiscus or a bean flower for insect pollination, maize tassel and silk or grass for wind). Collect fruits and seeds from the compound for dispersal: blackjack, jacaranda, a bean pod, a mango.

skills.key_step: The child names the parts of a flower and their functions (sepals protect, petals attract, stamen of anther and filament is male, carpel of stigma, style and ovary is female) and the role of flowers in nature (seeds, fruit, food for animals).

floor.prerequisite: Knows the jobs of the flower parts from Grade 5.
floor.question: Which part holds the pollen?

representations: a chart: part, male or female, job
steps: Role: seeds and fruits; food for insects, birds and people.

board.say: Male or female, and what is it called?

board.do: Ask the child to label the stamen parts.

misconceptions.ask: What happens to the petals after pollination?
What does a bean flower become?
misconceptions.repair: Flowers make seeds and feed animals.

checks.question: Name the male part of a flower.
Give one role of flowers in nature.
checks.answer: they make seeds and fruits, or feed insects with nectar

skills.key_step: The child describes pollination (pollen from an anther to a stigma, self or cross) and the adaptations of wind-pollinated flowers (small, dull, feathery stigmas, much light pollen) and insect-pollinated ones (bright petals, scent, nectar, sticky pollen).

floor.prerequisite: Can name the parts of a flower.
floor.question: Which part receives pollen?

representations: a maize tassel and a hibiscus side by side
steps: Self: same flower or plant; cross: another plant.
Wind flowers: feathery stigmas, light pollen, no bright petals.
Insect flowers: bright, scented, nectar, sticky pollen.

board.do: Draw a maize tassel and a hibiscus.

board.say: Why is it long and feathery?

board.do: Wait for "to catch pollen from the wind".
Ask the child to list the insect features of the hibiscus.

misconceptions.ask: Which comes first: pollen landing, or cells joining?
misconceptions.repair: Pollination is pollen reaching a stigma.

misconceptions.ask: Does a maize tassel have bright petals?
misconceptions.repair: Wind flowers have feathery stigmas and light pollen.
Insect flowers are bright and scented.

misconceptions.ask: Can a bean flower pollinate itself?

checks.question: Give two features of a wind-pollinated flower.
checks.answer: any two: feathery stigma, much light pollen, small dull petals, no nectar

checks.question: What is cross-pollination?
checks.answer: pollen from one plant reaching the stigma of another plant of the same kind

skills.key_step: The child explains fertilisation (a pollen tube grows to the ovule and the male cell joins the egg), says the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit, and sorts fruits and seeds by their dispersal (wind: wings, hairs; animals: hooks, juicy; water: floats; explosion: pods burst).
representations: a collection of fruits and seeds
a flow chart from pollination to fruit
steps: Pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
Fertilisation: ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit.
Look at the fruit or seed: wing, hair, hook, juicy, float, pod.

board.do: Draw a blackjack seed with hooks and a jacaranda seed with a wing.
Wait for "by animals, it hooks onto fur".
Ask the child to draw a water-dispersed fruit.

misconceptions.ask: In a bean pod, which part was the ovary?
How many beans in one pod?

misconceptions.repair: Wind seeds have wings or hairs.

misconceptions.ask: What did the coconut husk do in the basin?

checks.question: Which part of a flower becomes the seed?
How are seeds with hooks dispersed?
checks.answer: by animals (they hook onto fur or clothes)
